what: Cactus makes wellheads and pressure control equipment for oil and gas wells, and spoolable pipe used to move oil, gas and water across well sites. In 2025 it agreed to take control of Baker Hughes’ surface pressure control business, adding international and offshore customers.
customers: US shale producers, and through the Baker Hughes deal, oil companies in the Middle East and offshore.
money: Wellheads and frac equipment sold and rented to drillers.
Flexible pipe for oil, gas and water gathering on well sites.
moat: Cactus designs wellheads that save drilling time, and it is known for fast service. That reputation, plus a lean cost base, has let it take share from much larger rivals in US shale.
risks: Demand follows the number of wells drilled in the US, which falls when oil prices drop.
The Baker Hughes deal brings integration risk and lower-margin international work.
Tariffs on steel and on parts from Asia raise costs.
Net income fell from $185M in 2024 to $166M in 2025.
opportunities: Debt of just $36M against $354M of cash: an unusually strong balance sheet for an oilfield company.
Revenue over the last twelve months reached $1.53B, well above 2025’s $1.08B, as the acquisition adds sales.
International markets give growth beyond US shale.
Nine analysts average a target near $72, about 27% above the price.
watch: Integration of the Baker Hughes business, and US rig counts.
view: Cactus has been one of the best-run companies in oilfield services: it took share in US shale with a better wellhead and faster service, kept costs lean and avoided debt. The trailing P/E of 39 overstates its cost because earnings are temporarily held down by deal costs; on forward estimates it is about 17.

The Baker Hughes deal is the turning point. It roughly doubles exposure to markets outside US shale, which is good diversification but lower margin and harder to run. Revenue already shows it, up to $1.53 billion over the last twelve months.

This turns on whether Cactus can bring the acquired business up to its own margins. Management has earned the benefit of the doubt, and the balance sheet means a mistake will not be fatal. I would call it fairly priced, and attractive if US drilling activity picks up.
bull: The acquired business reaches Cactus-level margins, international growth adds to a US recovery.
bear: US drilling stays weak and the acquisition dilutes returns.
